t6sd-sizing: In standard hold'em, 1/3-pot, half-pot, and 2/3-pot sizes are widely used. In short deck some "traditional sizes" fail or need adjustment: because draw density is high and made-hand value is large, half-pot/small bets may not protect your made hands (opponents draw too cheaply), while big bets/overbets are more effective when made-hand value is high.

Short-deck sizing rule: with high draw density, small bets can't protect made hands; with high made-hand value (flushes/straights), big bets/overbets extract more. Use big sizes for protection on wet boards; small thin-value bets are fine on dry boards.

Short-deck value:bluff ratio for bet sizes (formulas unchanged):
Bluff share f = b/(1+2b)
1/3 pot → 20%; half pot → 25%; full pot → 33%; 2× pot → 40%

Short-deck adjustments:
1. Wet boards (many draws) → big sizes (2/3 pot+) to protect made hands and charge draws
2. Dry boards → small sizes (1/3 pot) for thin value
3. High made-hand value (flushes/straights) → overbets can extract more

The essence of "traditional small bets failing": small bets give draws too cheap a price, and short-deck draws get there easily — you must protect with big sizes. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker bet sizing and 6+ protection)

Short-deck sizing practice: because pots are usually bigger and draw density high, sizing trends larger overall — use 2/3 pot or even full pot to protect made hands and charge draws. But also account for stack depth (SPR): deep stacks build pots with big sizes, shallow stacks are more direct. In short deck, "small thin-value bets" are often an error on wet boards.

Example: Short deck, you hold K♠K♦ on a 9♦8♣6♥ flop (wet, 98 connected). Your overpair is easily outdrawn by straights/two pair on a wet board, and opponent draw density is high. Use a 2/3+ pot big bet (pot 6, bet 4+) to protect — charge the opponent's straight/flush draws rather than giving a cheap price. A half-pot small bet isn't enough to protect an overpair on a wet short-deck board.

Example 2 (dry-board small bet): Short-deck flop K♠7♦J♣ (relatively dry), you hold A♠K♣. The opponent rarely hits this board; use a 1/3-pot small thin-value bet — weak hands in a wide range pay and junk folds, so small works. Small bets still work on dry boards; only wet boards need big sizes.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck "small thin-value bets" aren't always right. On wet boards (high draw density), a small bet gives draws too cheap a price — effectively letting the opponent chase for free. Short-deck draws get there easily, so you must protect with big sizes. Small bets are only right on dry boards.

Short-deck sizing quick memory: wet boards → 2/3+ pot big bets to protect made hands; dry boards → 1/3-pot small thin-value bets; high made-hand value (flushes/straights) → overbets to extract. First judge board wetness, then choose the size.
t6sd-barrel: Barreling is more frequent in short deck than standard hold'em because made-hand value is high and strong made hands (flushes/straights) need multiple streets to extract. Short-deck pros fire three barrels on strong hands like flushes/straights/two pair, building the pot with big sizes every street to extract full value. But when the board changes hands (turn/river completes the opponent's draws), adjust frequency.

Short-deck consecutive value-barrel rule: fire three barrels with strong made hands (flushes/straights/two pair) to extract value; but lower frequency when the turn/river changes hands (completes the opponent's draws). Value betting is more frequent but not mindless.

Short-deck consecutive value-bet pot geometry (starting pot P):
Three barrels (2/3 pot each street):
Flop 2/3P → turn 2/3×new pot → river 2/3×new pot

With P=6:
Flop bet 4, pot 14
Turn bet 9.3, pot 32.7
River bet 21.8, pot 76.2

Deep-stacked, strong made hands need big sizes so the pot grows geometrically and the shove lands on the river.

Board-change adjustment:
If the turn/river completes the opponent's draw (e.g. a straight/flush card), lower firing frequency and switch to pot control. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker multi-street value betting)

Short-deck barreling practice: because flush/straight made-hand value is high and draw density is large, short-deck value betting is more frequent — but the key is "barrel strong hands", not "barrel mindlessly". Dry boards allow three barrels (the opponent rarely hits), while wet boards that complete the opponent's draws (a flush/straight card on the turn) call for reducing frequency.

Example: Short deck, you hold A♠K♠ and flop top pair of Aces on a K♠7♦J♣ flop (relatively dry). You bet 1/3 pot, he calls. Turn 6♥ (semi-blank), you continue with a half-pot bet (top-pair value). River 9♣ (semi-blank), you bet 2/3 pot for value. Three streets of consecutive value betting because the board stays dry and the opponent rarely hits.

Example 2 (board change): Short deck, you hold 7♠8♠ on a 8♦9♣T♥ flop (open-ended straight draw), you semi-bluff bet and he calls. Turn 6♠ — completes your straight (6-7-8-9-T)! Now you make a straight and continue betting for value. But if the turn were J♦ (the opponent with Q-J makes a bigger straight, and 6-7 chops with you), you must assess whether he also made a straight and adjust when the board changes hands.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck consecutive value betting is more frequent, but "the board changing hands" matters more than your hand strength. When the turn/river completes the opponent's draw (a flush/straight card), even if you're still ahead, lower frequency — because the combos in his range that beat you have multiplied.

Short-deck barreling three questions: (1) whose draw does this board improve? (2) how many streets does my made hand need to extract? (3) can the pot geometry support an all-in? After three questions: barrel strong hands, pot-control when the board changes hands.
t6sd-equity-realization: Short-Deck Equity Realization: the Gap Between the Quote and the Payout

The standard-track chapter "Board Structure and Equity Realization" already fixes the terms: realized equity = all-in equity x realization rate, and the rate equals 1 if and only if the hand goes all-in immediately — after which nothing can force you to abandon it. This chapter does not re-derive that. It swaps the input to a 36-card deck and follows where the same back-solve lands.

Each out is worth more in short deck, yet there are fewer of them to count:

Marginal equity of one out: after the flop 1 / 31 = 3.2%, after the turn 1 / 30 = 3.3%
Holdem for comparison: 1 / 47 = 2.1%, 1 / 46 = 2.2%

Outs on a flush draw: short deck 5 (9 cards per suit minus 4 already visible) = 30.1% over two streets; holdem 9 = 35.0% over two streets

A single short-deck out is worth roughly 1.5 holdem outs — but the flush draw only has five of them.

So short deck does not mean "draws are worth more". The real relationship is: every card that helps you is more valuable, there are fewer of them to count, and the net effect is that a draw sits about five points lower in all-in equity. Importing the holdem 9-out instinct records 30.1% as 35.0%, and that single error straddles the half-pot threshold — so it costs real money.
What the realization rate turns 30.1% into

Worked example (the half-pot line): pot 8, opponent bets 4, threshold = 4 / 16 = 25.0%. On the flop your flush draw quotes 30.1% all-in, a margin of 5.1 points. If the hand has to survive three streets and you are forced off it on the turn, take a realization rate of 0.85: 30.1% x 0.85 = 25.6%, leaving six tenths of a point. At the same price with the same hand, the decision no longer lives in the draw — it lives in whether you still get to act afterwards.

Back-solving the threshold (this side is deck-independent):

Minimum all-in equity you can call with = threshold equity / realization rate

Half-pot threshold 25.0% / 0.85 = 29.4%  ->  the short-deck flush draw at 30.1% just clears it
Half-pot threshold 25.0% / 0.80 = 31.3%  ->  one notch worse in realization and it no longer does
Pot-size threshold 33.3% / 0.85 = 39.2%  ->  30.1% fails on the raw quote, discount or no discount

The realization rate is not a property of the deck but of whether this hand survives to showdown, so it is set by position, initiative and how messy the later streets are. Short deck raises the weight of all three: made hands are stronger and the board turns over more often (see the "Continuous Betting" chapter at this level), so falling behind is harder to recover from and being ahead is easier to overtake with one card. Carrying equity to the end is itself worth more.

Worked example (a pair is further ahead, and no safer): on a short-deck turn you hold a pair against a flush draw, one street to come, five outs against you, so you lead 1 - 5 / 31 = 83.9%; the same spot in holdem is 1 - 9 / 47 = 80.9%. That sounds like good news, and the reverse is equally true — when you challenge a pair with a draw, short deck is more completely dead to one card, with four fewer outs to save you.

Counter-intuitive point: "weaker" and "more valuable" hold at the same time in short-deck draws. Each out carries about 1.5 times the marginal equity of a holdem out, yet only five of them exist, so total equity is lower while every individual card matters more. That is precisely why short-deck draws live on the raise-and-shove branch rather than the call branch.
Which line sizing pushes a draw into

One short-deck flush draw (30.1% quoted over two streets), read three ways:

Pot 8, bet 4 (half pot): threshold 25.0% — the quote clears, and 25.6% after a 0.85 realization still scrapes by
Pot 8, bet 8 (pot size): threshold 8 / 24 = 33.3% — the quote is already 3.2 points short, so the realization rate never gets a vote
The same pot-size threshold against holdem 9 outs at 35.0%: still 1.6 points to spare

One and the same pot-size bet lets a draw through in holdem and turns it away in short deck. The interaction between sizing and deck lives in those few points.

Worked example (reverse the relationship instead of calling): facing a pot-size bet on a short-deck flop, calling pays a 33.3% threshold with a 30.1% quote, before any realization discount — the call is mispriced on its own terms. Only two honest options remain: raise to push the opponent fold rate up (the semi-bluff accounting is in the "Bluff Frequency" chapter at this level), or accept that this hand has no call branch at this size. "Call and see the turn" is not a compromise, it is paying for the same mistake twice.

One line to keep: short deck pays more per out (3.2% against 2.1%) and gives the flush draw fewer of them (5 against 9); the realization rate turns a 30.1% quote into a 25.6% payout, and the two back-solved lines — 29.4% and 39.2% — are the thresholds that actually decide a call. A stronger made hand is never an excuse for a cheaper draw.

Review checklist for short deck: check only three inputs — did you count outs against nine cards per suit, did you use 31/30 unknown cards rather than 47/46, and did position and later streets eat your realization rate. Get those right before discussing frequency or sizing, because almost every "something feels wrong in short deck" traces back to one of these three.

t6sd-sizing-q1.question: The essence of short-deck "traditional small bets failing" is:
options: Small bets give draws too cheap a price, and short-deck draws get there easily
t6sd-sizing-q1.explanation: Short-deck draw density is high and draws get there easily; small bets give draws too cheap a price and can't protect made hands.

t6sd-sizing-q2.question: Holding an overpair on a wet short-deck board (many draws), the correct size is:
options: 2/3+ pot big bet to protect the made hand
t6sd-sizing-q2.explanation: An overpair on a wet board is easily outdrawn and draw density is high — use a 2/3+ pot big bet to protect and charge draws.

t6sd-sizing-q3.question: Holding top pair on a relatively dry short-deck board (K♠7♦J♣), the correct size is:
t6sd-sizing-q3.explanation: The opponent rarely hits a dry board; a 1/3-pot small thin-value bet works, getting wide-range weak hands to pay.

t6sd-sizing-q4.question: Why do short-deck bet sizes trend larger overall?
options: Big pots + high draw density require big sizes to protect made hands and extract value
t6sd-sizing-q4.explanation: Short-deck pots are big and draw density is high — big sizes are needed to protect made hands, charge draws, and extract value.

t6sd-barrel-q1.question: Why is consecutive value betting more frequent in short deck than standard hold'em?
options: Made-hand value is high and strong made hands need multiple streets to extract
t6sd-barrel-q1.explanation: Short-deck flushes/straights and similar made hands are highly valuable and need consecutive streets of betting to extract full value.

t6sd-barrel-q2.question: Holding top pair on a relatively dry short-deck board (K♠7♦J♣→6♥→9♣), the correct betting line is:
options: Three barrels — the board stays dry and the opponent rarely hits
Big bets on turn and river
t6sd-barrel-q2.explanation: On a dry board the turn/river don't improve the opponent's draws and your top pair stays ahead — three barrels collect full value.

t6sd-barrel-q3.question: When the turn/river completes the opponent's draw in short deck (board changes hands), the correct adjustment is:
options: Lower firing frequency and switch to pot control
t6sd-barrel-q3.explanation: When the board changes hands (completes the opponent's draws), the combos beating you multiply — lower frequency and pot-control.

t6sd-barrel-q4.question: Deep-stacked in short deck, consecutive betting with strong made hands requires:
options: Big sizes so the pot grows geometrically and the shove lands on the river
t6sd-barrel-q4.explanation: Deep-stacked, strong made hands need big sizes to grow the pot geometrically street by street and complete the all-in on the river.

t6sd-barrel-q5.question: "The board changing hands matters more than your hand strength" means:
options: When the turn/river completes the opponent's draws, lower frequency even if you're ahead
No need to watch the board
t6sd-barrel-q5.explanation: When the board changes hands, the combos beating you multiply — lower firing frequency even if you're still ahead.

t6sd-equity-realization-q1.question: In short deck, the marginal equity of one out after the flop is about:
t6sd-equity-realization-q1.explanation: Only 31 cards remain unknown after a short-deck flop, so one out is 1 / 31 = 3.2%; holdem gives 1 / 47 = 2.1%.

t6sd-equity-realization-q2.question: How does the exact two-street equity of a short-deck flush draw (5 outs) compare with holdem 9 outs?
t6sd-equity-realization-q2.explanation: 1 - (26/31)(25/30) = 30.1% against 1 - (38/47)(37/46) = 35.0%: each out is worth more, but there are four fewer of them.

t6sd-equity-realization-q3.question: Pot 8 facing a pot-size bet of 8. The equity needed to call is:
t6sd-equity-realization-q3.explanation: Amount to call over the pot after calling: 8 / 24 = 33.3%, independent of the deck.

t6sd-equity-realization-q4.question: An all-in equity of 30.1% realized at a rate of 0.85 is about:
t6sd-equity-realization-q4.explanation: Realized equity = all-in equity x realization rate = 30.1% x 0.85 = 25.6%, leaving six tenths of a point of half-pot margin.

t6sd-equity-realization-q5.question: Facing a pot-size bet on a short-deck flop with a flush draw, the correct read is:
options: Call, since a flush is worth so much
The raw quote already fails: 30.1% is under the 33.3% threshold
Fold, since you have zero outs
Raise to double pot to make up the equity
t6sd-equity-realization-q5.explanation: The pot-size threshold is 8 / 24 = 33.3% while the two-street quote is 30.1%, so the call is mispriced before any discount.
